title: حِكَايَةُ الْقَرَنْدَلِيِّ الْأَوَّلِ
titleEn: The Tale of the First Qalandar
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 1, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 73–79 (continuing directly from nights-10, whose text ends as the lady of the house summons armed slaves to bind and behead her guests), transcribed from the 300 ppi scan (archive.org aliflailaorbooko01macn) by the project’s own two-pass-plus-adjudication pipeline; the edition’s own OCR is unusable. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition’s — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm exactly as Macnaghten prints it. Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition’s Middle Arabic forms and its occasional compositor’s slips, is preserved unaltered; a few genuinely obscure or corrupt-looking forms are vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes rather than silently repaired. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized automatically once this file is published, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 11 opens with the porter's fatal question still hanging: the lady of the house, cut off mid-laugh, rounds on her guests, and the Caliph's party (still disguised) buys a moment's grace by having each qalandar and the porter tell how he came to be there. This gives way to the night's main story, the Tale of the First Qalandar: a prince, inseparable from his cousin, is sworn to help him slip nightly into a hidden underground tomb-enclosure to visit a woman the cousin has fallen for and hidden away. The prince obliges, seals the vault as instructed, and returns to find, next morning, that he cannot locate the tomb-enclosure again by daylight — his cousin has vanished. Searching brings him home to find his own father overthrown and killed by a treacherous vizier, who — for the accidental loss of one eye, years before, to the prince's stray shot — orders the prince blinded and beheaded; the executioner, once his father's own man, spares his life instead and sends him fleeing into exile with two poems on betrayed loyalty. Reaching his uncle's city, he learns his cousin is still missing; uncle and nephew together relocate the tomb-enclosure, descend, and find the cousin and the woman burned to charred coal in a final embrace — the uncle spits on his son's blackened face, cursing him to the torment of the world to come, as dawn cuts Shahrazad off. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularized the language toward Classical Arabic here and there, so some of the original Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit. The night is frank about violence (an eye put out by order, an execution ordered and averted, a corpse burned and spat upon) and is translated that way, without euphemism.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ الْحَادِيَةَ عَشَرَ قَالَتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُ أَنَّ الصَّبِيَّةَ لَمَّا ضَحِكَتْ مِنْ غَيْظِهَا أَقْبَلَتْ عَلَى الْجَمَاعَةِ وَ قَالَتْ أَخْبِرُونِي بِخَبَرِكُم
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānat al-laylatu al-ḥādiyata ʿashara qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu anna al-ṣabiyyata lammā ḍaḥikat min ghayẓihā aqbalat ʿalā al-jamāʿati wa-qālat akhbirūnī bi-khabarikum
sentences.l: Then, when it was the eleventh night, she said: It has reached me, O fortunate King, that the young lady — when she had laughed off her rage — turned to the company and said, 'Tell me your news.'
sentences.i: When the eleventh night came, she said: As I have heard, O fortunate King, the young lady, having laughed away her anger, turned to the assembled company and said, 'Tell me your tidings.'
sentences.n: الحادية عشر prints without the agreeing تاء one would expect on عشرة for a feminine night (compare اللَّيْلَةُ الْعَاشِرَةُ the night before); compound ordinals of this kind are often frozen this way, and it is vocalized here as printed. 'The young lady' is the mistress of the house who has been questioning her guests since the close of the previous night.

sentences.t: فَمَا بَقِيَ مِنْ أَعْمَارِكُم إِلَّا سَاعَةٌ وَلَوْلَا أَنْتُم عَزِيزِينَ أَوْ أَكَابِرَ قَوْمِكُم أَوْ خَدَمًا لَمَّا كُنْتُم تَجَارَيْتُم
sentences.tr: fa-mā baqiya min aʿmārikum illā sāʿatun wa-lawlā antum ʿazīzīna aw akābira qawmikum aw khadaman lamā kuntum tajāraytum
sentences.l: For there remains of your lives naught but an hour; and were you not honored guests, or great men of your people, or servants, you would not have fared as you have.
sentences.i: Only an hour remains to each of you of your lives; and were you not men of honor, or great ones among your own people, or servants, you would not have gotten off so lightly.
sentences.n: لولا ... لما is the classical pattern 'were it not for X, Y would not have happened' — the لما here is this same response particle (lamā), not the temporal lammā. تجاريتم (from جرى, 'to run, get on') most likely means 'you would have fared, gotten on [with us]'; the precise nuance of the verb in this idiom is uncertain.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ الْخَلِيفَةُ وَيْلَكَ يَا جَعْفَرُ أَخْبِرْهَا بِنَا وَإِلَّا
sentences.tr: fa-qāla al-khalīfatu waylaka yā Jaʿfaru akhbirhā binā wa-illā
sentences.l: Then the Caliph said: 'Woe to you, O Jafar — tell her about us, or else —'
sentences.i: Then the Caliph said, 'Confound you, Jafar! Tell her who we are, or else—'
sentences.n: This is Hārūn al-Rashīd, still in his merchant disguise with his vizier Jaʿfar; وإلا breaks off before the threat is completed, a common device of this narration.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا غَلِطَا وَحَسَّنَ لَهَا الْخَوَلُ قَبْلَ أَنْ يَحِلَّ بِنَا الْمَكْرُوهُ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā ghaliṭā wa-ḥassana lahā al-khawalu qabla an yaḥilla binā al-makrūhu
sentences.l: For the two of them had already blundered, and the retinue had smoothed things over for her, before harm should befall us —
sentences.i: For the two of us have already overstepped, and it is only the household's soothing of her that has kept trouble from falling on us so far —
sentences.n: This clause is one of the passage's genuine difficulties. 'غلطا' (dual, 'the two of them erred') most likely refers to the Caliph and Jaʿfar having pressed their luck as guests; the exact reference and sense of 'الخول' smoothing things over is not fully certain, and this is offered as the best available reading, vocalized exactly as printed.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ جَعْفَرُ مِنْ بَعْضِ مَا تَسْتَأْهِلُ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla Jaʿfaru min baʿḍi mā tastaʾhilu
sentences.l: Then Jafar said: 'Of some of what she deserves.'
sentences.i: Jafar answered, 'Only a little of what she has coming to her.'
sentences.n: Jaʿfar deflects with a flippant remark rather than answering the Caliph's demand, which draws the rebuke that follows.

sentences.t: فَزَعَقَ عَلَيْهِ الْخَلِيفَةُ وَ قَالَ الْهَزْلُ لَهُ وَقْتٌ وَالْجِدُّ لَهُ وَقْتٌ
sentences.tr: fa-zaʿaqa ʿalayhi al-khalīfatu wa-qāla al-hazlu lahu waqtun wa-al-jiddu lahu waqtun
sentences.l: So the Caliph shouted at him, and said: 'Jesting has its time, and earnestness has its time.'
sentences.i: The Caliph rounded on him and said, 'There is a time for jesting, and a time for being in earnest!'

sentences.t: هَذَا وَالصَّبِيَّةُ أَقْبَلَتْ عَلَى الْقَرَنْدَلِيَّةِ وَقَالَتْ لَهُم أَنْتُم إِخْوَةٌ
sentences.tr: hādhā wa-al-ṣabiyyatu aqbalat ʿalā al-qarandaliyyati wa-qālat lahum antum ikhwatun
sentences.l: So much for that. And the young lady turned to the qalandars and said to them: 'Are you brothers?'
sentences.i: So much for that. Meanwhile the young lady turned to the qalandars and said to them, 'Are you brothers, all of you?'
sentences.n: هذا here closes off the Caliph-and-Jaʿfar exchange before the narration returns to the lady of the house; القرندلية names the three one-eyed qalandars as a group.

sentences.t: قَالُوا لَا وَاللَّهِ مَا نَحْنُ إِلَّا فُقَرَاءُ وَ أَعْجَامٌ
sentences.tr: qālū lā wa-Allāhi mā naḥnu illā fuqarāʾu wa-aʿjāmun
sentences.l: They said: 'No, by God — we are nothing but poor men and foreigners.'
sentences.i: 'No, by God,' they said, 'we are only poor men, foreigners every one.'
sentences.n: أعجام, 'non-Arabs, foreigners', is their claimed excuse for being strangers to one another rather than kin.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ لِوَاحِدٍ مِنْهُم أَنْتَ أَعْوَرُ وُلِدْتَ
sentences.tr: fa-qālat li-wāḥidin minhum anta aʿwaru wulidta
sentences.l: Then she said to one of them: 'Were you born one-eyed?'
sentences.i: Then she said to one of them, 'Were you born blind in that eye?'

sentences.t: قَالَ لَا وَاللَّهِ أَنَا قَدْ جَرَى لِي حَدِيثٌ عَجِيبٌ وَأَمْرٌ غَرِيبٌ لَمَّا قَلَعْتُ عَيْنِي وَلِي حِكَايَةٌ لَوْ كُتِبَتْ بِالْإِبَرِ عَلَى آمَاقِ الْبَصَرِ لَصَارَتْ عِبْرَةً لِمَنْ اِعْتَبَرَ
sentences.tr: qāla lā wa-Allāhi anā qad jarā lī ḥadīthun ʿajībun wa-amrun gharībun lammā qalaʿtu ʿaynī wa-lī ḥikāyatun law kutibat bi-al-ibari ʿalā āmāqi al-baṣari la-ṣārat ʿibratan li-man iʿtabara
sentences.l: He said: 'No, by God — a strange happening and a curious matter befell me when I plucked out my eye; and I have a story which, were it written with needles upon the corners of the eye, would become a lesson to whoever took heed.'
sentences.i: 'No, by God,' he said. 'A strange thing befell me, and a curious matter, when I plucked out my eye; and I have a tale that, were it written with needles on the corners of the eye, would stand as a lesson to any who took it to heart.'
sentences.n: 'Written with needles on the corners of the eye' is a set formula of hyperbolic wonder that recurs at several points across the Nights, marking what follows as an extraordinary tale.

sentences.t: قَالَ وَسَأَلْتُ الثَّانِيَ وَالثَّالِثَ فَقَالُوا مِثْلَ الْأَوَّلِ
sentences.tr: qāla wa-saʾaltu al-thāniya wa-al-thālitha fa-qālū mithla al-awwali
sentences.l: She said: 'And I asked the second and the third, and they said the like of the first.'
sentences.i: She went on: 'I asked the second and the third as well, and they answered just as the first had.'
sentences.n: قَالَ is unmarked for gender here; context makes the speaker the lady of the house, continuing in her own words to report that she put the same question to the other two qalandars — the same loose gender-marking seen elsewhere in this text (compare فَضَحِكَ below).

sentences.t: وَقَالُوا وَاللَّهِ يَا مَوْلَاتَنَا كُلُّ وَاحِدٍ مِنَّا مِنْ بَلَدٍ وَابْنُ مَلِكٍ وَحَاكِمٌ عَلَى بِلَادٍ وَعِبَادٍ
sentences.tr: wa-qālū wa-Allāhi yā mawlātanā kullu wāḥidin minnā min baladin wa-ibnu malikin wa-ḥākimun ʿalā bilādin wa-ʿibādin
sentences.l: And they said: 'By God, O our mistress, each one of us is from a [different] city, and a son of a king, and a ruler over lands and subjects.'
sentences.i: And they said, 'By God, our lady, each of us comes from a different city; each is a king's son, and a ruler over lands and subjects.'

sentences.t: فَالْتَفَتَتِ الصَّبِيَّةُ لَهُم وَقَالَتْ كُلُّ وَاحِدٍ مِنْكُم يَحْكِي عَلَيَّ حِكَايَتَهُ وَمَا سَبَبُ مَجِيئِهِ إِلَى عِنْدَنَا يُمَلِّسُ عَلَى رَأْسِهِ وَيَرُوحُ إِلَى حَالِ سَبِيلِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-iltafatat al-ṣabiyyatu lahum wa-qālat kullu wāḥidin minkum yaḥkī ʿalayya ḥikāyatahu wa-mā sababa majīʾihi ilā ʿindanā yumallisu ʿalā raʾsihi wa-yarūḥu ilā ḥāli sabīlihi
sentences.l: So the young lady turned to them and said: 'Let each one of you tell me his story, and the reason for his coming to us — [then] let him wipe his head and go on his own way.'
sentences.i: The young lady turned to them and said, 'Let each of you tell me his tale, and the reason he came to us — and then he may be on his way.'
sentences.n: 'يملس على راسه ويروح', literally 'wipe his head and go', is the same colloquial idiom of dismissal already used of the porter, and used of him again a few lines further on.

sentences.t: فَأَوَّلُ مَا تَقَدَّمَ الْحَمَّالُ
sentences.tr: fa-awwalu mā taqaddama al-ḥammālu
sentences.l: So the first to come forward was the porter.
sentences.i: The first to step forward was the porter.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ يَا سِتِّي أَنَا رَجُلٌ حَمَّالٌ حَمَلَتْنِي هَذِهِ الْخَوْشَكَاشَةُ وَجَاءَتْ بِي مِنْ بَيْتِ النَّبَّاذِ إِلَى دُكَّانِ الْجَزَّارِ وَمِنْ دُكَّانِ الْجَزَّارِ إِلَى الْفَاكِهَانِيِّ وَمِنْ عِنْدِةِ إِلَى النَّقْلِيِّ وَمِنْ النَّقْلِيِّ إِلَى الْحَلْوَانِيِّ وَالْعَطَّارِ وَمِنْهُ إِلَى هُنَا وَجَرَى لِي مَعَكُم مَا جَرَى وَهَذَا حَدِيثِي وَالسَّلَامُ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla yā sittī anā rajulun ḥammālun ḥamalatnī hādhihi al-khawshakāshatu wa-jāʾat bī min bayti al-nabbādhi ilā dukkāni al-jazzāri wa-min dukkāni al-jazzāri ilā al-fākihāniyyi wa-min ʿindihi ilā al-naqliyyi wa-min al-naqliyyi ilā al-ḥalwāniyyi wa-al-ʿaṭṭāri wa-minhu ilā hunā wa-jarā lī maʿakum mā jarā wa-hādhā ḥadīthī wa-al-salām
sentences.l: He said: 'O my lady, I am a man, a porter. This Khushkasha hired me, and she brought me from the wine-house to the shop of the butcher, and from the shop of the butcher to the fruiterer, and from him to the nut-seller, and from the nut-seller to the confectioner and the grocer, and from him to here; and there befell me with you what befell me; and this is my story, and that's all.'
sentences.i: He said, 'My lady, I am nothing but a porter. This Khushkasha here hired me and led me from the wine-shop to the butcher's stall, and from the butcher's stall to the fruit-seller's, and from him to the nut-seller's, and from the nut-seller's to the confectioner's and the grocer's, and from there to here; and what has passed between us here has passed. That is my whole story — and that is that.'
sentences.n: النباذ، الجزار، الفاكهاني، النقلي، الحلواني، العطار are all trade-names rather than proper names — the wine-seller, the butcher, the fruiterer, the nut- or dried-fruit seller, the confectioner and the grocer/perfumer — naming the chain of Baghdad shops the porter has just come from; والسلام closing a speech is a colloquial 'and that's that', not the greeting formula.

sentences.t: فَضَحِكَ الصَّبِيَّةُ وَقَالَتْ لَهُ مَلِّسْ عَلَى رَأْسِكَ وَرُحْ
sentences.tr: fa-ḍaḥika al-ṣabiyyatu wa-qālat lahu mallis ʿalā raʾsika wa-ruḥ
sentences.l: So the young lady laughed, and said to him: 'Wipe your head, and go.'
sentences.i: At this the young lady laughed, and said to him, 'Off with you, then — be on your way.'
sentences.n: ضحك is printed in the masculine although its subject الصبية is feminine — the same loose gender agreement met elsewhere in this text's Middle Arabic; vocalized here exactly as printed.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ وَاللَّهِ مَا أَرُوحُ حَتَّى أَسْمَعَ حَدِيثَ رُفَقَائِي
sentences.tr: fa-qāla wa-Allāhi mā arūḥu ḥattā asmaʿa ḥadītha rufaqāʾī
sentences.l: He said: 'By God, I will not go until I hear the story of my companions.'
sentences.i: He said, 'By God, I will not stir until I have heard my companions' tale.'

sentences.t: فَتَقَدَّمَ الْقَرَنْدَلِيُّ الْأَوَّلُ وَقَالَ لَهَا يَا سِتِّي اِعْلَمِي أَنَّ سَبَبَ حَلْقِ ذَقْنِي وَقَلْعِ عَيْنِي أَنَّ وَالِدِي كَانَ مَلِكً وَلَهُ أَخٌ وَ كَانَ أَخُوهُ مَلِكً فِي مَدِينَةٍ أُخْرَى
sentences.tr: fa-taqaddama al-qarandalīyu al-awwalu wa-qāla lahā yā sittī iʿlamī anna sababa ḥalqi dhaqnī wa-qalʿi ʿaynī anna wālidī kāna malikan wa-lahu akhun wa-kāna akhūhu malikan fī madīnatin ukhrā
sentences.l: So the first qalandar came forward, and said to her: 'O my lady, know that the reason for the shaving of my chin and the plucking out of my eye [is] that my father was a king, and he had a brother; and his brother was king in another city.'
sentences.i: Then the first qalandar stepped forward and said to her, 'My lady, know that the reason my chin was shaved and my eye put out is this: my father was a king, and he had a brother, who was king in another city.'
sentences.n: 'Shaving the chin' names the qalandars' distinctive tonsure (beard and eyebrows shaved smooth), the mark of this order of wandering dervishes. The sentence embeds one أنّ-clause inside another — 'the reason ... [is] that ...' — kept exactly as it stands.

sentences.t: وَاتَّفَقَ أَنَّ أُمِّي وَلَدَتْنِي وَوُلِدَ ابْنُ عَمِّي فِي يَوْمٍ وَاحِدٍ
sentences.tr: wa-ittafaqa anna ummī waladatnī wa-wulida ibnu ʿammī fī yawmin wāḥidin
sentences.l: And it so happened that my mother bore me, and my cousin was born, on one and the same day.
sentences.i: And it so happened that my mother gave birth to me, and my cousin was born, on that very same day.

sentences.t: وَمَضَتْ سِنِينَ وَأَعْوَامٌ وَأَيَّامٌ حَتَّى كَبِرْنَا
sentences.tr: wa-maḍat sinīna wa-aʿwāmun wa-ayyāmun ḥattā kabirnā
sentences.l: And there passed years and years and days, until we grew up.
sentences.i: Years and years and days went by, until we came of age.
sentences.n: سنين، أعوام، أيام piles up three near-synonyms for 'time passing', a doubling and tripling this prose favors for emphasis; سنين keeps its oblique plural shape here even as grammatical subject, a case-leveling common to this text's Middle Arabic.

sentences.t: وَكُنْتُ أَزُورُ عَمِّي فِي كُلِّ قَلِيلٍ وَأَقْعُدُ عِنْدَةُ أَشْهُرًا عَدِيدَةً فَأَكْرَمَنِي ابْنُ عَمِّي غَايَةَ الْإِكْرَامِ وَذَبَحَ لِي الْأَغْنَامَ وَرَوَّقَ لِي الْمُدَامَ
sentences.tr: wa-kuntu azūru ʿammī fī kulli qalīlin wa-aqʿudu ʿindahu ashhuran ʿadīdatan fa-akramanī ibnu ʿammī ghāyata al-ikrāmi wa-dhabaḥa lī al-aghnāma wa-rawwaqa lī al-mudāma
sentences.l: And I used to visit my uncle every little while, and stay with him for many months; and my cousin honored me with the utmost of honoring, and slaughtered for me the sheep, and strained for me the wine.
sentences.i: I used to visit my uncle now and again, and stay with him for months at a stretch; and my cousin would honor me most lavishly — he would slaughter sheep for me and have wine strained for my sake.
sentences.n: عندة here spells the pronoun 'him' with a tāʾ marbūṭa rather than the expected ه — a genuine Middle Arabic orthographic habit found elsewhere in this edition, kept exactly as printed. غاية الإكرام, 'the utmost of honoring', is the same intensifying construction met in the frame story's غَايَةَ الْفَرَحِ.

sentences.t: وَجَلَسْنَا لِلشَّرَابِ
sentences.tr: wa-jalasnā li-al-sharābi
sentences.l: And we sat down to the wine.
sentences.i: And we sat down together to drink.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا تَحَكَّمَ الشَّرَابُ مِنَّا قَالَ لِي ابْنُ عَمِّي يَا ابْنَ عَمِّي لِي إِلَيْكَ حَاجَةٌ مُهِمَّةٌ وَأُرِيدُ أَنْ لَا تُخَالِفَنِي فِيمَا أُرِيدُ أَنْ أَفْعَلَهُ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā taḥakkama al-sharābu minnā qāla lī ibnu ʿammī yā ibna ʿammī lī ilayka ḥājatun muhimmatun wa-urīdu an lā tukhālifanī fīmā urīdu an afʿalahu
sentences.l: And when the wine had gained mastery over us, my cousin said to me: 'O my cousin, I have to you an important need, and I want that you not oppose me in what I want that I do it,'
sentences.i: And when the wine had taken hold of us, my cousin said to me, 'Cousin, I have an urgent need of you, and I want you not to cross me in what I mean to do,'

sentences.t: فَقُلْتُ لَهُ حُبًّا وَكَرَامَةً
sentences.tr: fa-qultu lahu ḥubban wa-karāmatan
sentences.l: so I said to him, love and honor.
sentences.i: so I said to him, 'Most gladly.'
sentences.n: حبا وكرامة (ḥubban wa-karāmatan), lit. 'love and honor,' is a fixed idiom of willing consent — 'gladly, with all my heart.'

sentences.t: فَاسْتَوْثَقَ مِنِّي بِالْأَيْمَانِ الْعِظَامِ وَنَهَضَ مِنْ وَقْتِهِ وَ سَاعَتِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-istawthaqa minnī bi-al-aymāni al-ʿiẕāmi wa-nahaḍa min waqtihi wa-sāʿatihi
sentences.l: So he made-sure of me with the-oaths the-mighty, and he arose from his-time and his-hour.
sentences.i: So he bound me fast with solemn oaths, and rose at once, that very moment.
sentences.n: من وقته وساعته (min waqtihi wa-sāʿatihi) is an idiom of immediacy: 'on the instant, without delay.'

sentences.t: وَغَابَ قَلِيلًا وَعَادَ وَخَلْفَهُ اِمْرَأَةٌ مُتَزَيِّنَةٌ مُطَيَّبَةٌ وَعَلَيْهَا مِنَ الْحُلَلِ مَا يُسَاوِي مَبْلَغًا عَظِيمًا
sentences.tr: wa-ghāba qalīlan wa-ʿāda wa-khalfahu imraʾatun mutazayyinatun muṭayyabatun wa-ʿalayhā mina al-ḥulali mā yusāwī mablaghan ʿaẕīman
sentences.l: And he was-absent a-little, and he returned, and behind-him a-woman adorned, perfumed, and upon-her from the-robes what equals a-sum great.
sentences.i: He was gone a little while, then came back, and behind him walked a woman, adorned and perfumed, wearing robes worth a fortune.

sentences.t: فَالْتَفَتَ إِلَيَّ وَالْمَرْأَةُ خَلْفَهُ وَقَالَ خُذْ هٰذِهِ الْمَرْأَةَ وَاسْبِقْنِي عَلَى الْجَبَّانَةِ الْفُلَانِيَّةِ
sentences.tr: fa-iltafata ilayya wa-al-marʾatu khalfahu wa-qāla khudh hādhihi al-marʾata wa-isbiqnī ʿalā al-jabbānati al-fulāniyyati
sentences.l: Then he turned to me, the-woman [being] behind-him, and he said, 'Take this the-woman, and precede-me to the-burial-ground the-such-and-such.'
sentences.i: Then he turned to me, the woman standing behind him, and said, 'Take this woman, and go ahead of me to such-and-such a burial-ground.'
sentences.n: الفلانية (al-fulāniyyah), 'the so-and-so [one],' is a deliberately vague placeholder name, a common storytelling device for withholding a real name.

sentences.t: وَصَفَهَا لِي فَعَرَفْتُهَا
sentences.tr: waṣafahā lī fa-ʿaraftuhā
sentences.l: He described her to me, so I knew her.
sentences.i: He described it to me, so that I recognized it.
sentences.n: The pronoun '-hā' (her/it) refers back to the graveyard, itself grammatically feminine, not to the woman. There is no separate 'and' here: وَصَفَهَا is a single word, the verb وَصَفَ ('describe') plus the object suffix, its initial و being part of the root, not a conjunction.

sentences.t: وَ قَالَ لِي ادْخُلْ بِهَا إِلَى التُّرْبَةِ وَانْتَظِرْ لِي هُنَاكَ
sentences.tr: wa-qāla lī udkhul bihā ilā al-turbati wa-intaẕir lī hunāka
sentences.l: And he said to me, 'Enter with-her into the-tomb-enclosure, and wait for-me there.'
sentences.i: And he said to me, 'Go in with her into the tomb-enclosure, and wait for me there.'
sentences.n: التربة (al-turbah) here names a walled burial-ground or family vault, not a single grave — the individual قبر (grave) inside it is mentioned separately below.

sentences.t: فَلَمْ يُمْكِنْنِي الْمُخَالَفَةُ وَلَمْ أَقْدِرْ أَرُدَّ سُؤَالَهُ لِأَجْلِ الْيَمِينِ الَّذِي حَلَفْتُهُ
sentences.tr: fa-lam yumkinnī al-mukhālafatu wa-lam aqdir arudda suʾālahu li-ajli al-yamīni alladhī ḥalaftuhu
sentences.l: So not was-possible-for-me the-opposing, and not was-I-able [that] I-refuse his-request, for-the-sake-of the-oath which I-had-sworn-it.
sentences.i: So I could not oppose him, nor was I able to refuse his request, because of the oath I had sworn.

sentences.t: فَأَخَذْتُ الْمَرْأَةَ وَسِرْتُ إِلَى أَنْ دَخَلْتُ التُّرْبَةَ أَنَا وَإِيَّاهَا
sentences.tr: fa-akhadhtu al-marʾata wa-sirtu ilā an dakhaltu al-turbata anā wa-iyyāhā
sentences.l: So I took the-woman, and I went until [that] I entered the-tomb, I and her(self).
sentences.i: So I took the woman and went on until I entered the tomb-enclosure, she and I together.
sentences.n: أنا وإيّاها (anā wa-iyyāhā) coordinates the subject pronoun 'I' with the object pronoun 'her' via the disjunctive pronoun إيّا — a normal way to say 'she and I together.'

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا اسْتَقَرَّ بِنَا الْجُلُوسُ جَاءَ اِبْنُ عَمِّي وَمَعَهُ طَاسَةٌ فِيهَا مَاءٌ وَكِيسٌ فِيهِ جِبْسٌ وَقَدُومٌ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā istaqarra binā al-julūsu jāʾa ibnu ʿammī wa-maʿahu ṭāsatun fīhā māʾun wa-kīsun fīhi jibsun wa-qadūmun
sentences.l: Then when settled with-us the-sitting, came [the]-son of-my-uncle, and with-him a-basin, in-it water, and a-bag, in-it plaster, and an-adze.
sentences.i: Then, once we had settled ourselves sitting there, my cousin arrived, carrying a basin of water, a bag of plaster, and a pick-axe.
sentences.n: قدوم (qadūm) is a heavy tool for digging or hewing stone — an adze or mattock, here used to open the grave.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّهُ أَخَذَ الْقَدُومَ وَجَاءَ إِلَى قَبْرٍ فِي وَسَطِ التُّرْبَةِ فَفَكَّهُ وَنَقَلَ أَحْجَارَهُ إِلَى نَاحِيَةِ التُّرْبَةِ
sentences.tr: thumma innahu akhadha al-qadūma wa-jāʾa ilā qabrin fī wasaṭi al-turbati fa-fakkahu wa-naqala aḥjārahu ilā nāḥiyati al-turbati
sentences.l: Then indeed-he took the-adze, and he came to a-grave in [the]-middle-of the-tomb-enclosure, and-he-undid-it, and he moved its-stones to [the]-side-of the-tomb-enclosure.
sentences.i: Then he took up the pick-axe and went to a grave in the middle of the tomb-enclosure; he broke it open and carried its stones off to one side of the enclosure.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ بَحَثَ بِالْقَدُومِ فِي أَرْضِ الْقَبْرِ ثُمَّ انْكَشَفَ عَنْ طَابَقٍ حَدِيدٍ قَدْرَ الْبَابِ الصَّغِيرِ فِي الْأَرْضِ
sentences.tr: thumma baḥatha bi-al-qadūmi fī arḍi al-qabri thumma inkashafa ʿan ṭābaqin ḥadīdin qadra al-bābi al-ṣaghīri fī al-arḍi
sentences.l: Then he dug with the-adze in [the]-ground of the-grave, then was-uncovered from an-iron slab, [the]-size-of the-door the-small, in the-ground.
sentences.i: Then he dug with the pick into the floor of the grave, until an iron slab, the size of a small door, lay uncovered in the earth.
sentences.n: طابق (ṭābaq) here means a covering slab or trapdoor (lit. 'a layer'), not the modern sense of 'storey.'

sentences.t: فَشَالَهُ فَبَانَ مِنْ تَحْتِهِ سُلَّمٌ مَعْقُودٌ ثُمَّ الْتَفَتَ إِلَى الْمَرْأَةِ وَقَالَ لَهَا دُونَكِ وَمَا تَخْتَارِي
sentences.tr: fa-shālahu fa-bāna min taḥtihi sullamun maʿqūdun thumma iltafata ilā al-marʾati wa-qāla lahā dūnaki wa-mā takhtārī
sentences.l: So he lifted-it, then appeared from beneath-it a-staircase built. Then he turned to the-woman and said to-her, 'Here-you-are, and whatever you-choose.'
sentences.i: So he lifted it, and beneath it a staircase came into view. Then he turned to the woman and said to her, 'Here you are — take what you will.'
sentences.n: معقود (maʿqūd), lit. 'knotted/vaulted,' describing the staircase, is left uncertain here — perhaps 'built into the earth' or 'spiral'; the exact construction is not clear. دونك (dūnaki) is an old idiom meaning roughly 'here, take it, it is yours to choose.' تختاري (takhtārī) drops the expected final ن of the classical feminine imperfect (takhtārīna) — a regular feature of this Middle Arabic, not a slip.

sentences.t: فَنَزَلَتْ الْمَرْأَةُ مِنْ ذٰلِكَ السُّلَّمِ
sentences.tr: fa-nazalat al-marʾatu min dhālika al-sullami
sentences.l: So went-down the-woman from that the-staircase.
sentences.i: So the woman climbed down that staircase.

sentences.t: فَالْتَفَتَ إِلَيَّ وَقَالَ يَا اِبْنَ عَمِّي تَمَامُ الْمَعْرُوفِ إِذَا نَزَلْتُ أَنَا فِي ذٰلِكَ الْمَوْضِعِ رُدَّ الطَّابَقَ وَرُدَّ عَلَيْهِ التُّرَابَ كَمَا كَانَ عَلَى الطَّابَقِ
sentences.tr: fa-iltafata ilayya wa-qāla yā ibna ʿammī tamāmu al-maʿrūfi idhā nazaltu anā fī dhālika al-mawḍiʿi rudda al-ṭābaqa wa-rudda ʿalayhi al-turāba kamā kāna ʿalā al-ṭābaqi
sentences.l: Then he turned to me and said, 'O son of my-uncle, [the]-completion of the-kindness: when I-go-down, I, in that the-place, put-back the-slab, and put-back upon-it the-earth as it-was upon the-slab.'
sentences.i: Then he turned to me and said, 'O my cousin, here is the rest of the favor I ask: once I have gone down into that place, put the slab back, and heap the earth over it just as it lay upon the slab before.'
sentences.n: تمام المعروف (tamām al-maʿrūf), 'the completion of the kindness,' is a set phrase introducing the final and most important part of a request.

sentences.t: وَهٰذَا تَمَامُ الْمَعْرُوفِ وَهٰذَا الْجِبْسُ الَّذِي فِي الْكِيسِ وَهٰذَا الْمَاءُ الَّذِي فِي الطَّاسَةِ اِعْجِنْ بِهِ الْجِبْسَ
sentences.tr: wa-hādhā tamāmu al-maʿrūfi wa-hādhā al-jibsu alladhī fī al-kīsi wa-hādhā al-māʾu alladhī fī al-ṭāsati iʿjin bihi al-jibsa
sentences.l: And this [is the] completion of the-kindness, and this the-plaster which [is] in the-bag, and this the-water which [is] in the-basin: knead with-it the-plaster.
sentences.i: And this is the rest of the favor: here is the plaster in the bag, and here is the water in the basin — knead the plaster with it.

sentences.t: وَلَبِسَ الْقَبْرَ كَمَا كَانَ أَوَّلًا فِي دَائِرِ الْأَحْجَارِ حَتَّى لَا يَرَاهَا أَحَدٌ وَيَقُولُ هٰذَا فَتْحٌ جَدِيدٌ وَبَطْنُهُ عَتِيقٌ
sentences.tr: wa-labisa al-qabra kamā kāna awwalan fī dāʾiri al-aḥjāri ḥattā lā yarāhā aḥadun wa-yaqūlu hādhā fatḥun jadīdun wa-baṭnuhu ʿatīqun
sentences.l: And he-clothed(-plastered) the-grave as it-was at-first, in [the]-ring-of the-stones, so-that not sees-it anyone, and says, 'This [is] an-opening new, and its-belly [is] old.'
sentences.i: And plaster over the grave, around the ring of stones, just as it was before, so that no one may see it and say, 'Here is a fresh breach, though what lies beneath is old.'
sentences.n: The edition prints ولبس with no initial alif at all, so this cannot be the imperative اِلْبِسِ (which needs one); read as it stands it is the plain past tense لَبِسَ, 'and he clothed/coated [it],' continuing the instruction with a bare perfect used for imperative force — a vernacular feature, not a copying slip. Separately, the referent of '-hā' in يراها is left implicit — most naturally the plastered patch itself, since the grave, القبر, is grammatically masculine.

sentences.t: لِأَنَّ لِي سَنَةٌ كَامِلَةٌ وَأَنَا أَعْمَلُ فِيهِ وَمَا يَعْلَمُ بِي إِلَّا اللَّهُ
sentences.tr: li-anna lī sanatun kāmilatun wa-anā aʿmalu fīhi wa-mā yaʿlamu bī illā Allāhu
sentences.l: Because to-me [is] a-year complete, and I [have-been] working in-it, and not knows of-me except God.
sentences.i: For I have spent a full year at this work, and none knows of me save God.

sentences.t: وَ هٰذِهِ حَاجَتِي إِلَيْكَ
sentences.tr: wa-hādhihi ḥājatī ilayka
sentences.l: And this [is] my-need to you.
sentences.i: And this is my request of you.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ قَالَ لِي لَا أَوْحَشَ اللَّهُ مِنْكَ يَا اِبْنَ عَمِّي
sentences.tr: thumma qāla lī lā awḥasha Allāhu minka yā ibna ʿammī
sentences.l: Then he said to me, 'Not may-He-make-desolate, God, from you, O son of my-uncle!'
sentences.i: Then he said to me, 'God grant I never be without you, O my cousin!'
sentences.n: لا أوحش الله منك (lā awḥasha Allāhu minka) is a fixed parting-blessing, lit. 'may God not make [me] desolate of you' — roughly 'may I never lack you,' said on taking leave.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ نَزَلَ فِي السُّلَّمِ
sentences.tr: thumma nazala fī al-sullami
sentences.l: Then he went down the staircase.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا غَابَ عَنْ عَيْنِي قُمْتُ وَرَدَّيْتُ الطَّابَقَ وَفَعَلْتُ مَا أَمَرَنِي بِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā ghāba ʿan ʿaynī qumtu wa-raddaytu al-ṭābaqa wa-faʿaltu mā amaranī bihi
sentences.l: Then when he-vanished from my-eye(sight), I-arose, and I-put-back the-slab, and I-did what he-had-commanded-me with-it.
sentences.i: Then, when he had vanished from my sight, I rose, put the slab back, and did as he had bidden me.
sentences.n: ردّيت (raddaytu) for classical رددت (radadtu, 'I put back'): Middle Arabic here conjugates the doubled root ر-د-د as though it were a defective (weak) verb, giving a -ayt ending instead of the expected geminate -adt. The meaning is unaffected.

sentences.t: وَبَقِيَ الْقَبْرُ كَمَا كَانَ وَأَنَا فِي خُمَارِ سَكْرَانَ
sentences.tr: wa-baqiya al-qabru kamā kāna wa-anā fī khumāri sakrāna
sentences.l: And remained the-grave as it-was, while-I [was] in [the]-daze-of a-drunk-man.
sentences.i: And the grave stayed just as it had been, while I moved about as though I were drunk.
sentences.n: خمار سكران (khumār sakrān), lit. 'a drunkard's fuddled daze,' describes bewilderment or shock, not literal drinking.

sentences.t: وَرَجَعْتُ إِلَى قَصْرِ عَمِّي وَكَانَ عَمِّي فِي الصَّيْدِ وَالْقَنَصِ
sentences.tr: wa-rajaʿtu ilā qaṣri ʿammī wa-kāna ʿammī fī al-ṣaydi wa-al-qanaṣi
sentences.l: And I returned to [the]-palace of-my-uncle, and was my-uncle at the-hunting and the-chasing.
sentences.i: And I returned to my uncle's palace; and my uncle was out hunting, in pursuit of game.
sentences.n: الصيد والقنص (al-ṣayd wa-al-qanaṣ), 'the hunting and the chase,' pairs two near-synonyms for emphasis, a common stylistic doubling.

sentences.t: فَنِمْتُ تِلْكَ اللَّيْلَةَ
sentences.tr: fa-nimtu tilka al-laylata
sentences.l: So I slept that night.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا أَصْبَحَ الصَّبَاحُ تَفَكَّرْتُ اللَّيْلَهَ الْمَاضِيَةَ وَمَا جَرَى فِيهَا عَلَى ابْنِ عَمِّي
sentences.tr: fa-lammā aṣbaḥa al-ṣabāḥu tafakkartu al-laylata al-māḍiyata wa-mā jarā fīhā ʿalā ibni ʿammī
sentences.l: Then when the morning came, I pondered the past night, and what had happened in it, concerning my cousin (my paternal-uncle's-son).
sentences.i: Then, when morning came, I thought over the events of the past night, and what had befallen my cousin.
sentences.n: أَصْبَحَ الصَّبَاحُ, literally 'the morning became-morning,' is a stock way of opening a new day's narration; ابْنُ عَمٍّ, 'son of a paternal uncle,' is simply 'cousin.' The edition spells اللَّيْلَة with a final هـ instead of ة, as it often does; it is still read al-laylata.

sentences.t: وَنَدِمْتُ حَيْثُ لَا يَنْفَعُ النَّدَمُ عَلَى مَا فَعَلْتُ مَعَهُ وَطَاوَعْتُهُ فَظَنَنْتُ أَنَّهُ كَانَ مَنَامًا
sentences.tr: wa-nadimtu ḥaythu lā yanfaʿu al-nadamu ʿalā mā faʿaltu maʿahu wa-ṭāwaʿtuhu fa-ẕanantu annahu kāna manāman
sentences.l: And I repented — where regret avails not — over what I had done with him and had complied with him; and I supposed that it had been a dream.
sentences.i: And I repented, though regret was no use to me now, for what I had done and for having gone along with him; and I told myself it had all been a dream.
sentences.n: حَيْثُ لَا يَنْفَعُ النَّدَمُ, 'where regret is of no avail,' is a fixed lament for something already beyond undoing.

sentences.t: فَالْتَفَتُّ عَنِ ابْنِ عَمِّي فَمَا كَانَ أَحَدٌ يُخْبِرُنِي عَنْهُ
sentences.tr: fa-iltafattu ʿani ibni ʿammī fa-mā kāna aḥadun yukhbirunī ʿanhu
sentences.l: So I turned about concerning my cousin, but there was no one to inform me about him.
sentences.i: So I turned to ask after my cousin, but there was no one to tell me anything of him.

sentences.t: فَخَرَجْتُ إِلَى الْمَقَابِرِ وَالْجَبَّانَةِ وَفَتَّشْتُ عَلَى التُّرْبَةِ فَلَمْ أَعْرِفْهَا
sentences.tr: fa-kharajtu ilā al-maqābiri wa-al-jabbānati wa-fattashtu ʿalā al-turbati fa-lam aʿrifhā
sentences.l: So I went out to the graves and the burial-ground, and I searched over the grave-plot, but I did not recognize it.
sentences.i: So I went out to the graves and the burial-ground and searched among the plots, but I could not tell which one it was.
sentences.n: الْمَقَابِر and الْجَبَّانَة, 'the graves' and 'the burial-ground,' are near-synonyms paired for emphasis, as this style often does; التُّرْبَة, literally 'the earth, the soil,' here means the particular grave-plot the narrator is hunting for.

sentences.t: وَ لَمْ أَزَلْ أَدُورُ تُرْبَةً تُرْبَةً وَقَبْرًا قَبْرًا حَتَّى أَقْبَلَ اللَّيْلُ وَلَمْ أَهْتَدِ عَلَيْهَا
sentences.tr: wa-lam azal adūru turbatan turbatan wa-qabran qabran ḥattā aqbala al-laylu wa-lam ahtadi ʿalayhā
sentences.l: And I did not cease going-around, plot by plot and grave by grave, until the night came on, and I was not guided to it.
sentences.i: I kept going from plot to plot and grave to grave, until night fell, and still I could not find my way to it.
sentences.n: لَمْ أَزَلْ + imperfect ('I did not cease doing') is this narrator's way of saying 'I kept on doing'; تُرْبَةً تُرْبَةً and قَبْرًا قَبْرًا repeat the noun in the accusative to mean 'one after another, plot by plot.'

sentences.t: فَرَجَعْتُ إِلَى الْقَصْرِ وَلَمْ آكُلْ وَلَمْ أَشْرَبْ وَقَدِ اشْتَغَلَ خَاطِرِي بِابْنِ عَمِّي بِحَيْثُ لَا أَعْلَمُ لَهُ حَالًا
sentences.tr: fa-rajaʿtu ilā al-qaṣri wa-lam ākul wa-lam ashrab wa-qadi ishtaghala khāṭirī bi-ibni ʿammī bi-ḥaythu lā aʿlamu lahu ḥālan
sentences.l: So I returned to the palace, and I did not eat and I did not drink, for my mind had become occupied with my cousin, such that I knew no state for him.
sentences.i: So I went back to the palace, and I neither ate nor drank, for my mind was so taken up with my cousin that I had no notion of what had become of him.
sentences.n: خَاطِرِي, 'my mind, my thoughts,' is common in this register for one's inward attention; بِحَيْثُ here means 'to the point that,' introducing a result. لَمْ آكُلْ is spelled in the edition with a single bare alif; the doubled hamza of 'I did not eat' (the person-prefix hamza plus the root's own) is written here with the combining madda that represents that contraction.

sentences.t: فَاغْتَمَمْتُ غَمًّا شَدِيدًا فَنِمْتُ لَيْلَتِي وَ بِتُّ مَهْمُومًا إِلَى الصَّبَاحِ
sentences.tr: fa-ightamamtu ghamman shadīdan fa-nimtu laylatī wa-bittu mahmūman ilā al-ṣabāḥi
sentences.l: So I grieved a violent grief, and I slept my night, and I spent-the-night care-worn, until the morning.
sentences.i: So I fell into violent grief. I went to sleep for the night, but passed it troubled, until morning.
sentences.n: بَاتَ means simply 'to spend the night,' not necessarily awake; it is regularly paired with a participle of state, as here with مَهْمُومًا, 'care-worn.'

sentences.t: فَجِئْتُ ثَانِيًا إِلَى الْجَبَّانَةِ وَأَنَا أُفَكِّرُ فِيمَا فَعَلَهُ ابْنُ عَمِّي وَنَدِمْتُ عَلَى سَمَاعِي مِنْهُ
sentences.tr: fa-jiʾtu thāniyan ilā al-jabbānati wa-anā ufakkiru fīmā faʿalahu ibnu ʿammī wa-nadimtu ʿalā samāʿī minhu
sentences.l: So I came a second time to the burial-ground, while I was pondering over what my cousin had done, and I repented of my listening to him.
sentences.i: So I went a second time to the burial-ground, turning over in my mind what my cousin had done, and repenting that I had ever listened to him.

sentences.t: وَقَدْ دُرْتُ فِي التُّرَبِ جَمِيعًا فَلَمْ أَعْرِفْ تِلْكَ التُّرْبَةَ وَذٰلِكَ الْقَبْرَ فَنَدِمْتُ عَلَى ذٰلِكَ
sentences.tr: wa-qad durtu fī al-turabi jamīʿan fa-lam aʿrif tilka al-turbata wa-dhālika al-qabra fa-nadimtu ʿalā dhālika
sentences.l: And I had gone-around among the grave-plots, all of them, but I did not recognize that grave-plot and that grave; so I repented over that.
sentences.i: I had gone the round of every plot, but I could not tell which plot, which grave, was the one; and I repented of it bitterly.

sentences.t: وَدُمْتُ عَلَى هٰذَا الْحَالِ سَبْعَةَ أَيَّامٍ فَلَمْ أَعْرِفْ لَهَا طَرِيقًا فَزَادَ بِي الْوَسْوَاسُ
sentences.tr: wa-dumtu ʿalā hādhā al-ḥāli sabʿata ayyāmin fa-lam aʿrif lahā ṭarīqan fa-zāda bī al-waswāsu
sentences.l: And I remained upon this state seven days, and I found for it no way, so obsessive-doubt increased in me.
sentences.i: I stayed in this condition seven days, and could find no way to it at all, until my mind grew ever more distracted with obsession.
sentences.n: الْوَسْوَاس, literally 'the whispering,' is the creeping obsession or anxiety that takes hold of someone — the same root that gives 'the Whisperer,' one of the Devil's epithets.

sentences.t: حَتَّى كِدْتُ أَنْ أَجُنَّ فَلَمْ أَجِدْ فَرَجًا دُونَ أَنْ سَافَرْتُ وَرَجَعْتُ إِلَى أَبِي
sentences.tr: ḥattā kidtu an ajunna fa-lam ajid farajan dūna an safartu wa-rajaʿtu ilā abī
sentences.l: until I nearly went-mad; and I found no relief-from-distress, except that I journeyed and returned to my father.
sentences.i: until I very nearly lost my mind; and I found no relief but to set out and go back to my father.
sentences.n: دُونَ أَنْ here means 'short of, without'; 'دون أن سافرت' is 'without my having journeyed' — i.e. 'only by setting out.'

sentences.t: فَسَاعَةَ وُصُولِي إِلَى مَدِينَةِ أَبِي نَهَضَ جَمَاعَةٌ عَلَى بَابِ الْمَدِينَةِ وَكَتَّفُونِي
sentences.tr: fa-sāʿata wuṣūlī ilā madīnati abī nahaḍa jamāʿatun ʿalā bābi al-madīnati wa-kattafūnī
sentences.l: So, the moment of my arrival at my father's city, a group rose up at the gate of the city and pinioned me.
sentences.i: The very moment I reached my father's city, a party of men rose up at the city gate and seized and bound me.
sentences.n: كَتَّفَ, literally 'to shoulder' someone, means to bind their arms behind their back.

sentences.t: فَتَعَجَّبْتُ كُلَّ الْعَجَبِ وَأَنَا ابْنُ سُلْطَانِ الْمَدِينَةِ وَهُمْ خَدَمُ أَبِي وَغِلْمَانِي
sentences.tr: fa-taʿajjabtu kulla al-ʿajabi wa-anā ibnu sulṭāni al-madīnati wa-hum khadamu abī wa-ghilmānī
sentences.l: So I wondered the whole of wondering — I being the son of the sultan of the city, and they my father's servants and my own pages.
sentences.i: I was utterly astonished, for I was the sultan's own son, and these men were my father's servants and my own retainers.
sentences.n: كُلَّ الْعَجَبِ, 'the whole of wonder,' is an intensifying idiom for 'the utmost astonishment.'

sentences.t: فَلَحِقَنِي مِنْهُمْ خَوْفٌ زَائِدٌ فَقُلْتُ فِي نَفْسِي يَا تُرَى مَا جَرَى عَلَى وَالِدِي
sentences.tr: fa-laḥiqanī minhum khawfun zāʾidun fa-qultu fī nafsī yā turā mā jarā ʿalā wālidī
sentences.l: So there overtook me, from them, an excessive fear; and I said within myself, 'Oh might-it-be-seen — what has happened to my father?'
sentences.i: A great fear of them came over me, and I said to myself, 'I wonder what has happened to my father!'
sentences.n: يَا تُرَى, literally 'oh, might it be seen,' is the fixed exclamation for 'I wonder…', opening a question addressed to oneself.

sentences.t: وَأَسْأَلُ الَّذِينَ مَسَكُونِي عَنْ سَبَبِ ذٰلِكَ فَلَمْ يَرُدُّوا عَلَىَّ جَوَابًا
sentences.tr: wa-asʾalu alladhīna masakūnī ʿan sababi dhālika fa-lam yaruddū ʿalayya jawāban
sentences.l: and I ask (I shall ask) those who had seized me about the reason for that; but they returned to me no answer.
sentences.i: and I would ask those who had laid hold of me the reason for it — but they gave me back no answer.
sentences.n: وَأَسْأَلُ switches to the imperfect ('I ask, I shall ask') inside this reported inner speech, where the surrounding narrative runs in the perfect — a common shift when a character's exact thought is being quoted. رَدَّ عَلَى/عَلَيَّ جَوَابًا is the fixed idiom 'to give someone an answer in reply'; the edition spells عَلَيَّ ('upon me') as عَلَى, using the letter ى where a word-final يّ is meant, a common economy in this book's typesetting.

sentences.t: فَبَعْدَ حِينٍ قَالَ لِي بَعْضُهُمْ وَكَانَ خَادِمًا عِنْدِي إِنَّ أَبَاكَ قَدْ غَدَرَ بِهِ الزَّمَانُ
sentences.tr: fa-baʿda ḥīnin qāla lī baʿḍuhum wa-kāna khādiman ʿindī inna abāka qad ghadara bihi al-zamānu
sentences.l: Then after a while, one of them said to me — and he had been a servant with me — 'Indeed your father, time has betrayed him.'
sentences.i: After a while, one of them — who had been a servant of mine — said to me, 'Truly, fortune has turned against your father.'
sentences.n: غَدَرَ بِهِ الزَّمَانُ, literally 'time/fortune betrayed him,' is a stock way of saying that someone's luck has turned disastrously.

sentences.t: وَخَامَرَ عَلَيْهِ الْعَسَاكِرُ وَقَتَلَهُ الْوَزِيرُ وَقَعَدَ مَكَانَهُ
sentences.tr: wa-khāmara ʿalayhi al-ʿasākiru wa-qatalahu al-wazīru wa-qaʿada makānahu
sentences.l: and the troops conspired against him, and the vizier killed him, and sat in his place.
sentences.i: the troops rose in conspiracy against him, and the vizier killed him and seated himself in his place.
sentences.n: خَامَرَ عَلَيْهِ, 'to conspire, to plot against someone,' is Form III used with عَلَى.

sentences.t: وَنَحْنُ نَتَرَقَّبُ لَكَ بِأَمْرِهِ
sentences.tr: wa-naḥnu nataraqqabu laka bi-amrihi
sentences.l: and we have been watching for you, by his order.
sentences.i: and we have been on the watch for you, at his command.

sentences.t: فَأَخَذُونِي وَأَنَا غَائِبٌ عَنِ الدُّنْيَا مِنْ هٰذِهِ الْأَخْبَارِ الَّتِي سَمِعْتُهَا عَنْ أَبِي
sentences.tr: fa-akhadhūnī wa-anā ghāʾibun ʿani al-dunyā min hādhihi al-akhbāri allatī samiʿtuhā ʿan abī
sentences.l: So they seized me, while I was absent from the world, at these tidings that I had heard concerning my father.
sentences.i: So they seized me while I stood as one absent from the world, at this news I had heard of my father.
sentences.n: غَائِبٌ عَنِ الدُّنْيَا, 'absent from the world,' describes the daze of hearing terrible news, as if one had momentarily left one's senses.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا تَمَثَّلْتُ بَيْنَ يَدَيْهِ وَكَانَ بَيْنِي وَبَيْنَ الْوَزِيرِ عَدَاوَةٌ قَدِيمَةٌ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā tamaththaltu bayna yadayhi wa-kāna baynī wa-bayna al-wazīri ʿadāwatun qadīmatun
sentences.l: Then, when I stood-presented before him — and there was, between me and the vizier, an old enmity —
sentences.i: When I was brought to stand before him — now there was an old enmity between me and the vizier —
sentences.n: تَمَثَّلَ بَيْنَ يَدَيْهِ, 'to present oneself, to stand before someone,' is the formal posture of standing before a ruler.

sentences.t: وَسَبَبُ تِلْكَ الْعَدَاوَةِ كُنْتُ مُولَعًا بِضَرْبِ قَوْسِ الْبُنْدُقِ
sentences.tr: wa-sababu tilka al-ʿadāwati kuntu mūlaʿan bi-ḍarbi qawsi al-bundaqi
sentences.l: and the cause of that enmity — I had been enamored of shooting the pellet-bow.
sentences.i: and the cause of that enmity was this: I had been passionately fond of shooting with the pellet-bow.
sentences.n: قَوْسُ الْبُنْدُقِ, the 'pellet-bow' or stone-bow, shoots small clay or lead pellets rather than arrows; it was a common hunting weapon.

sentences.t: وَإِذَا أَنَا يَوْمًا مِنَ الْأَيَّامِ وَاقِفٌ عَلَى سَطْحِ قَصْرِي
sentences.tr: wa-idhā anā yawman mina al-ayyāmi wāqifun ʿalā saṭḥi qaṣrī
sentences.l: And behold, I — one day, of the days — was standing on the roof of my palace.
sentences.i: And there I was, one day, standing on the roof of my palace.
sentences.n: وَإِذَا + pronoun + predicate is the 'idhā of surprise,' vividly presenting a scene exactly as the speaker found it: 'and suddenly, there I was…' You will meet it again just below, in the form وَإِذَا بِـ, marking something that suddenly appears.

sentences.t: وَإِذَا بِطَائِرٍ نَزَلَ عَلَى سَطْحِ قَصْرِ الْوَزِيرِ وَكَانَ وَاقِفًا
sentences.tr: wa-idhā bi-ṭāʾirin nazala ʿalā saṭḥi qaṣri al-wazīri wa-kāna wāqifan
sentences.l: And behold, with a bird that alighted on the roof of the vizier's palace — and he was standing there.
sentences.i: And suddenly a bird alighted on the roof of the vizier's palace — and the vizier himself happened to be standing there.
sentences.n: وَإِذَا بِـ, 'and behold, there was…', is the fixed idiom for something's sudden appearance; the بِـ marks what appears, not an instrument or a place — compare the glossary's وَإِذَا بِغَزَالَةٍ, 'and behold, a gazelle.'

sentences.t: فَأَرَدْتُ أَنْ أَضْرِبَ الطَّيْرَ وَإِذَا بِالْبُنْدُقَةِ أَخْطَأَتْ وَحَطَّتْ فِي عَيْنِ الْوَزِيرِ
sentences.tr: fa-aradtu an aḍriba al-ṭayra wa-idhā bi-al-bunduqati akhṭaʾat wa-ḥaṭṭat fī ʿayni al-wazīri
sentences.l: So I wanted to strike the bird; and behold, with the pellet — it went-astray, and it landed in the eye of the vizier.
sentences.i: So I made to shoot at the bird — and suddenly the pellet went astray and struck the vizier's eye.

sentences.t: قَلَعْتُهَا بِالْقَضَا وَالْقَدَرِ كَمَا قِيلَ فِي بَعْضِ الْأَمْثَالِ الْمَاضِيَةِ شِعْرٌ
sentences.tr: qalaʿtuhā bi-al-qaḍā wa-al-qadari kamā qīla fī baʿḍi al-amthāli al-māḍiyati shiʿrun
sentences.l: I put it out, by the decree and the destiny, as is said in some of the bygone proverbs — verse:
sentences.i: I put it out — his eye — by decree and destiny, as is said in one of the old proverbs, in verse:
sentences.n: قَلَعْتُهَا, 'I put it out,' refers back to الْعَيْن, 'the eye' (feminine), not to the pellet — the shot has cost the vizier his eye. بِالْقَضَا وَالْقَدَرِ, 'by decree and destiny,' is the standard formula for an event fated to happen; الْقَضَا is spelled here without its final hamza (for الْقَضَاءِ), a common simplification in this text. شِعْرٌ, 'verse,' is the manuscript's own rubric announcing that what follows is poetry, not narration.

sentences.t:
مَشَيْنَاهَا خُطًا كُتِبَتْ عَلَيْنَا * وَمَنْ كُتِبَتْ عَلَيْهِ خُطًا مَشَاهَا
وَمَنْ كَانَتْ مَنِيَّتُهُ بِاَرْضٍ * فَلَيْسَ يَمُوتُ فِي اَرْضٍ سِوَاهَا
sentences.tr:
mashaynāhā khuṭan kutibat ʿalaynā * wa-man kutibat ʿalayhi khuṭan mashāhā
wa-man kānat maniyyatuhu bi-arḍin * fa-laysa yamūtu fī arḍin siwāhā
sentences.l:
We walked paces that were written upon us; and he for whom paces were written, walked them.
And he whose death was appointed in a land — he does not die in a land other than it.
sentences.i:
We have walked the paces that were written for us; and whoever's paces are written, walks them.
And he whose death is destined for a certain land will never die in any land but that one.
sentences.n: A well-known proverb-couplet on fate, quoted mid-tale: what is decreed will surely come to pass. The word أَرْض, 'land,' is printed twice in the second line — بِاَرْضٍ and فِي اَرْضٍ — pointed with the vowel a hamza would carry (a fatḥa on the alif) but without the hamza sign itself; the verse is copied here exactly as the edition points it, without adding the missing hamza.

sentences.t: قَٰلَ الْقَرَنْدَلِيُّ فَلَمَّا اِنْقَلَعَتْ عَيْنُ الْوَزِيرِ لَمْ يَقْدِرْ يَتَكَلَّمَ لِأَنَّ وَالِدِي كَانَ مَلِكَ الْمَدِينَةِ فَهٰذَا سَبَبُ الْعَدَاوَةِ بَيْنِي وَبَيْنَهُ
sentences.tr: qāla al-qarandaliyyu fa-lammā inqalaʿat ʿaynu al-wazīri lam yaqdir yatakallama li-anna wālidī kāna malika al-madīnati fa-hādhā sababu al-ʿadāwati baynī wa-baynahu
sentences.l: The qalandar said: When the vizier's eye was plucked out, he was not able to speak, because my father was king of the city — so this is the cause of the enmity between me and him.
sentences.i: The qalandar said: When the vizier's eye was put out he dared not speak of it, for my father was king of that city — and this was the root of the enmity between him and me.
sentences.n: لَمْ يَقْدِرْ يَتَكَلَّمَ drops أَنْ before the verb it governs — the ordinary Middle-Arabic asyndetic construction met earlier in this text; read it simply as 'he could not speak.'

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا وَقَفْتُ قُدَّامَهُ وَأَنَا مُكَتَّفٌ أَمَرَ بِضَرْبِ عُنُقِي فَقُلْتُ لَهُ بِأَيِّ ذَنْبٍ تَقْتُلُنِي
sentences.tr: fa-lammā waqaftu quddāmahu wa-anā mukattafun amara bi-ḍarbi ʿunuqī fa-qultu lahu bi-ayyi dhanbin taqtulunī
sentences.l: Then when I stood before him, and I bound, he ordered the striking of my neck; so I said to him: for what crime do you kill me?
sentences.i: Then, when I stood before him with my arms pinioned, he gave the order to strike off my head; and I said to him, 'For what crime do you kill me?'

sentences.t: فَقَالَ أَيُّ ذَنْبٍ أَعْظَمُ مِنْ هٰذَا وَأَشَارَ إِلَى عَيْنِهِ الْمَقْلُوعَةِ فَقُلْتُ لَهُ هٰذَا فَعَلْتُهُ خَطَأً
sentences.tr: fa-qāla ayyu dhanbin aʿẓamu min hādhā wa-ashāra ilā ʿaynihi al-maqlūʿati fa-qultu lahu hādhā faʿaltuhu khaṭaʾan
sentences.l: So he said: what crime is greater than this? — and he pointed to his plucked-out eye. So I said to him: this — I did it by mistake.
sentences.i: He said, 'What crime is greater than this?' — and he pointed to his gouged-out eye. I said to him, 'That I did by accident.'
sentences.n: هٰذَا فَعَلْتُهُ topic-fronts the demonstrative ('this — I did it'), a normal Arabic word order that literal English keeps as a dash-set aside.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ إِنْ كُنْتَ فَعَلْتَهُ خَطَأً فَأَنَا أَفْعَلُهُ عَمْدًا ثُمَّ قَالَ قَدِّمُوهُ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla in kunta faʿaltahu khaṭaʾan fa-anā afʿaluhu ʿamdan thumma qāla qaddimūhu
sentences.l: So he said: if you did it by mistake, then I — I do it intentionally. Then he said: bring him forward!
sentences.i: He said, 'If you did it by mistake, then I do it by design.' Then he said, 'Bring him forward!'

sentences.t: فَقَدَّمُرْنِي بَيْنَ يَدَيْهِ فَمَدَّ أُصْبُعَهُ فِي عَيْنِي الْيُمْنَى قَلَعَهَا
sentences.tr: fa-qaddamurnī bayna yadayhi fa-madda uṣbuʿahu fī ʿaynī al-yumnā qalaʿahā
sentences.l: So they brought me forward before him, and he put his finger into my right eye [and] plucked it out.
sentences.i: So they brought me before him, and he thrust his finger into my right eye and tore it out.
sentences.n: The edition prints فقدمرني, one letter off from the sense's evident فَقَدَّمُونِي 'so they brought me forward' (و misread or misprinted as ر); vocalized here as printed and read by that intended verb.

sentences.t: فَصِرْتُ مِنْ ذٰلِكَ الْوَقْتِ أَعْوَرَ كَمَا نَرَوْنِی
sentences.tr: fa-ṣirtu min dhālika al-waqti aʿwara kamā narawnī
sentences.l: So I became, from that time, one-eyed, as you-see-me.
sentences.i: And from that hour I became one-eyed, as you see me now.
sentences.n: The edition prints نرونی (with a Persian-style dotless final ی), reading ن where the sense calls for تَرَوْنِي 'as you (all) see me' — most likely a single dot lost; vocalized here as printed but read by that intended تـ-form, the narrator's direct address to his listeners.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ كَتَفَنِي وَحَطَّنِي فِي صُنْدُوقٍ وَقَٰلَ لِلْسَّيَّافِ تَسَلَّمْ هٰذَا وَأَشْهِرْ حُسَامَكَ وَخُذْهُ وَاِذْهَبْ بِهِ إِلَى بَرِّ الْمَدِينَةِ وَاُقْتُلْهُ وَدَعِ الْوُحُوشَ وَالطُّيُورَ تَأْكُلُهُ
sentences.tr: thumma katafanī wa-ḥaṭṭanī fī ṣundūqin wa-qāla li-al-sayyāfi tasallam hādhā wa-ashhir ḥusāmaka wa-khudhhu wa-idhhab bihi ilā barri al-madīnati wa-uqtulhu wa-daʿi al-wuḥūsha wa-al-ṭuyūra taʾkuluhu
sentences.l: Then he pinioned me and put me in a chest, and he said to the executioner: 'Take charge of this one, and draw your sword, and take him, and go with him to the open country of the city, and kill him, and leave the wild beasts and the birds to eat him.'
sentences.i: Then he bound my arms and shut me in a chest, and said to the executioner, 'Take charge of this man; draw your blade, take him out to the open country beyond the city, kill him, and leave the wild beasts and the birds to devour him.'

sentences.t: فَخَرَجَ بِي السَّيَّافُ وَسَارَ حَتَّى خَرَجَ مِنَ الْمَدِينَةِ إِلَى وَسَطِ الْبَرِّيَّةِ وَأَخْرَجَنِي مِنَ الصُّنْدُوقِ
sentences.tr: fa-kharaja bī al-sayyāfu wa-sāra ḥattā kharaja mina al-madīnati ilā wasaṭi al-barriyyati wa-akhrajanī mina al-ṣundūqi
sentences.l: So the executioner went out with me, and journeyed, until he went out from the city into the middle of the wilderness, and took me out of the chest.
sentences.i: So the executioner led me forth and set out, until he had passed beyond the city into the heart of the wilderness; and there he took me out of the chest.

sentences.t: وَأَنَا مُكَتَّفُ الْيَدَيْنِ مَغْلُولُ الرِّجْلَيْنِ وَأَرَادَ أَنْ يَعْصِبَ عَيْنِي وَ يَقْتُلَنِي بَعْدَ ذٰلِكَ
sentences.tr: wa-anā mukattafu al-yadayni maghlūlu al-rijlayni wa-arāda an yaʿṣiba ʿaynī wa-yaqtulanī baʿda dhālika
sentences.l: And I [was] bound of the two hands, fettered of the two feet, and he intended to bind my eye and to kill me after that.
sentences.i: There I was, my hands pinioned and my feet shackled, and he meant to blindfold my one remaining eye and then kill me.

sentences.t: فَبَكَيْتُ بُكَاءًا شَدِيدًا حَتَّى أَبْكَيْتُهُ وَنَظَرْتُ إِلَيْهِ وَ أَنْشَدْتُ أَقُولُ هٰذَا الْأَبْيَاتَ شِعْرٌ
sentences.tr: fa-bakaytu bukāʾan shadīdan ḥattā abkaytuhu wa-naẓartu ilayhi wa-anshadtu aqūlu hādhā al-abyāta shiʿrun
sentences.l: So I wept a violent weeping until I made him weep; and I looked at him and recited, saying these verses — verse:
sentences.i: So I wept most bitterly, until I brought him too to tears; then I looked at him and recited these lines:
sentences.n: هٰذَا الْأَبْيَاتَ keeps the masculine demonstrative with the feminine plural noun الأبيات — a routine mismatch in this Middle Arabic prose, left as printed.

sentences.t:
حَسِبْتُكُمْ دِرْعًا حَصِينًا لِتَمْنَعُوا * سِهَامَ الْعِدَا عَنِّي فَكُنْتُمْ نِصَالَهَا
وَكُنْتُ ارْتَجِيكُمْ عِنْدَ كُلِّ مُلِمَّةٍ * اِذَا اَعْوَزَتْ اَيْدِي الْيَمِينِ شِمَالَهَا
دَعُوا قِصَّةَ الْعُذَّالِ عَنِّي بِمَعْزِلٍ * وَخَلُّوا الْعِدَا يَرْمُوا عَلَيَّ نِبَالَهَا
اِذَا اَنْتُمْ لَمْ تَنْصُرُونِي مِنَ الْعِدَا * فَكُنْتُمْ سَكَتُّمْ لَا عَلَيَّ وَلَا لَهَا
sentences.tr:
ḥasibtukum dirʿan ḥaṣīnan li-tamnaʿū * sihāma al-ʿidā ʿannī fa-kuntum niṣālahā
wa-kuntu artajīkum ʿinda kulli mulimmatin * idhā aʿwazat aydī al-yamīni shimālahā
daʿū qiṣṣata al-ʿudhdhāli ʿannī bi-maʿzilin * wa-khallū al-ʿidā yarmū ʿalayya nibālahā
idhā antum lam tanṣurūnī mina al-ʿidā * fa-kuntum sakattum lā ʿalayya wa-lā lahā
sentences.l:
I reckoned you a stout coat-of-mail to ward off the arrows of the enemies from me — but you became their [very] arrowheads.
And I used to hope in you at every calamity, when the right hands lacked their left [one hand needing the other].
Leave the story of the reproachers apart from me, and let the enemies fling their darts upon me.
If you do not aid me against the enemies, then be as you were — silent, neither for me nor against it.
sentences.i:
I took you for a coat of mail, proof against harm, to turn the enemy's arrows from me — but you turned into their very points.
I used to place my hope in you at every misfortune, as one right hand turns to its left when in need.
Spare me the talk of those who blame me, and let my enemies hurl their darts at me instead.
If you will not stand by me against my foes, then be at least silent — neither for me nor against me.
sentences.n: The four lines rhyme on -ālahā/-ā lahā (نِصَالَهَا، شِمَالَهَا، نِبَالَهَا، وَلَا لَهَا). The close, لَا عَلَيَّ وَلَا لَهَا, echoes the set idiom 'neither for it nor against it' — utter indifference; the Arabic itself leaves what لَهَا refers back to unstated.

sentences.t: وَقَالَ أَيْضًا شِعْرٌ
sentences.tr: wa-qāla ayḍan shiʿrun
sentences.l: And he said also, [in] verse:

sentences.t:
وَإِخْوَانٍ حَسِبْتُهُمْ دُرُوعاً * فَكَانُوهَا وَلَكِنْ لِلْاَعَادِي
وَظَنَنْتُهُمْ سِهَاماً صَائِبَاتٍ * فَكَانُوهَا وَلَكِنْ فِي فُؤَادِي
sentences.tr:
wa-ikhwānin ḥasibtuhum durūʿan * fa-kānūhā wa-lakin li-al-aʿādī
wa-ẓanantuhum sihāman ṣāʾibātin * fa-kānūhā wa-lakin fī fuʾādī
sentences.l:
And brothers I reckoned as coats-of-mail — and coats-of-mail indeed they became, but for the enemies.
And I thought them true-aimed arrows — and arrows indeed they became, but in my [own] heart.
sentences.i:
Brothers I once took for armor — armor indeed they proved to be, but armor worn against me.
I took them for well-aimed arrows — arrows indeed they proved, but arrows lodged in my own heart.
sentences.n: The same figure as the poem before it: those imagined as armor and as arrows turn out to be both, but turned against the speaker rather than for him.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَ السَّيَّافُ شِعْرِي وَكَانَ سَيَّافَ أَبِي وَلِي عَلَيْهِ الْإِحْسَانُ قَالَ يَا سَيِّدِي كَيْفَ أَفْعَلُ وَأَنَا عَبْدٌ مَأْمُورٌ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿa al-sayyāfu shiʿrī wa-kāna sayyāfa abī wa-lī ʿalayhi al-iḥsānu qāla yā sayyidī kayfa afʿalu wa-anā ʿabdun maʾmūrun
sentences.l: Then when the executioner heard my verse — and he had been my father's executioner, and to me was owed, upon him, the kindness — he said: O my master, how can I act, seeing I am a commanded slave?
sentences.i: When the executioner heard my verses — for he had been my father's executioner, and I had once done him a kindness — he said, 'My lord, what can I do? I am but a slave under orders.'
sentences.n: وَلِي عَلَيْهِ الْإِحْسَانُ, literally 'and to me, upon him, was the kindness,' is the idiom for having done someone a past favor now owed back.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ قَالَ لِي فُزْ بِعُمْرِكَ وَلَا تَجْعَلْ اِبْنَ هٰذِهِ الْأَرْضِ فَتَهْلَكَ وَتُهْلِكَنِي مَعَكَ كَمَا قَالَ بَعْضُهُمْ شِعْرٌ
sentences.tr: thumma qāla lī fuz bi-ʿumrika wa-lā tajʿal ibna hādhihi al-arḍi fa-tahlaka wa-tuhlikanī maʿaka kamā qāla baʿḍuhum shiʿrun
sentences.l: Then he said to me: escape with your life, and do not make [yourself] a son of this land, lest you perish and destroy me with you — as someone said, [in] verse:
sentences.i: Then he said to me, 'Save your life, and do not settle down here as though this land were your home, or you will perish and take me down with you' — as one of the poets has said:
sentences.n: فُزْ بِعُمْرِكَ, literally 'win with your life,' is the idiom for 'flee and save yourself.' اِبْنَ هٰذِهِ الْأَرْضِ, 'a son of this land,' means one who settles and belongs to a place — 'do not make yourself at home here.'

sentences.t:
وَنَفْسَكَ فُزْ بِهَا إِنْ صِبْتَ ضَيْماً * وَخَلِّ الدَّارَ تَنْعَى مَنْ بَنَاهَا
فَانَّكَ وَاجِدٌ اَرْضاً بِاَرْضٍ * وَنَفْسَكَ لَمْ تَجِدْ نَفْساً سِوَاهَا
عَجِبْتُ لِمَنْ يَعِيشُ بِدَارِ ذُلٍّ * وَاَرْضُ اللّٰهِ وَاسِعَةٌ فَلَاهَا
وَلَا تَبْعَثْ رَسُولَكَ فِي مُهِمٍّ * فَمَا لِلنَّفْسِ نَاصِحَةٌ خَلَاهَا
وَمَا غَلُظَتْ رِقَابُ الْأُسْلِ حَتَّى * بِأَنْفُسِهَا تَوَلَّتْ مِنْ عَنَاهَا
sentences.tr:
wa-nafsaka fuz bihā in ṣibta ḍayman * wa-khalli al-dāra tanʿā man banāhā
fa-annaka wājidun arḍan bi-arḍin * wa-nafsaka lam tajid nafsan siwāhā
ʿajibtu li-man yaʿīshu bi-dāri dhullin * wa-arḍu Allāhi wāsiʿatun fa-lāhā
wa-lā tabʿath rasūlaka fī muhimmin * fa-mā li-al-nafsi nāṣiḥatun khalāhā
wa-mā ghaluẓat riqābu al-usli ḥattā * bi-anfusihā tawallat min ʿanāhā
sentences.l:
And your soul — save it, if you meet with injustice; and leave the house to mourn the one who built it.
For indeed you will find a land in place of a land, but your soul — you will not find another soul instead of it.
I marvel at him who lives in a house of abasement, while God's earth is wide — so away from it!
And do not send your messenger on an urgent errand, for the self has no counselor apart from itself.
And the necks of the spears did not grow strong until, by themselves, they turned away from what wearied them.
sentences.i:
Save your own soul, if wrong befalls you, and leave the house to mourn the one who built it.
For you will find another land in place of this one, but you will never find another soul in place of your own.
I marvel at one who dwells in a house of disgrace, when God's earth lies wide open before him — let him forsake it!
Never send another on an errand that matters, for no one counsels the self as well as itself.
The shafts of the spears grew no stronger, until, of themselves, they turned away from what had worn them down.
sentences.n: Rhymes throughout on -āhā (بَنَاهَا، سِوَاهَا، فَلَاهَا، خَلَاهَا، عَنَاهَا). فَلَاهَا in the third line is obscure — no obvious sense from a root ل-و-ه/ل-ه-و fits here, and it looks chosen mainly for the rhyme; 'so away from it, forsake it' is a guess, not a settled reading. الْأُسْل is a poetic word for spear-shafts/lances; 'the necks of the lances' pictures their shafts as growing sound only through their own temper, closing the poem's theme of self-reliance.

sentences.t: فَقَبَّلْتُ يَدَيْهِ وَمَا صَدَّقْتُ بِالنَّجَاةِ وَهَانَ عَلَيَّ قَلْعُ عَيْنِي بِنَجَاتِي مِنَ الْقَتْلِ
sentences.tr: fa-qabbaltu yadayhi wa-mā ṣaddaqtu bi-al-najāti wa-hāna ʿalayya qalʿu ʿaynī bi-najātī min al-qatli
sentences.l: So I kissed his two hands, and I did not believe in the deliverance, and the plucking-out of my eye became easy for me, for my deliverance from being killed.
sentences.i: So I kissed his hands, scarcely believing I had truly escaped — the loss of my eye seemed a small price for being spared death.

sentences.t: وَسَافَرْتُ حَتَّى وَصَلْتُ إِلَى مَدِينَةِ عَمِّي فَدَخَلْتُ عَلَيْهِ وَأَعْلَمْتُهُ بِمَا جَرَى عَلَى وَالِدِي وَبِمَا جَرَى لِي مِنْ قَلْعِ عَيْنِي فَبَكَى بُكَاءً شَدِيدًا
sentences.tr: wa-sāfartu ḥattā waṣaltu ilā madīnati ʿammī fa-dakhaltu ʿalayhi wa-aʿlamtuhu bi-mā jarā ʿalā wālidī wa-bi-mā jarā lī min qalʿi ʿaynī fa-bakā bukāʾan shadīdan
sentences.l: And I traveled until I arrived at the city of my uncle, and I went in to him, and I informed him of what had happened to my father and of what had happened to me in the plucking-out of my eye; and he wept a violent weeping.
sentences.i: So I journeyed on until I reached my uncle's city, and went in to him, and told him what had befallen my father and what had befallen me in the loss of my eye. And he wept most bitterly.

sentences.t: وَقَالَ لَقَدْ زِدْتَنِي هَمًّا عَلَى هَمِّي وَغَمًّا عَلَى غَمِّي فَإِنَّ اِبْنَ عَمِّكَ قَلَّ عَالِمٌ وَلَا أَعْلَمُ مَا جَرَى عَلَيْهِ مُنْذُ أَيَّامٍ وَلَمْ يُخْبِرْنِي أَحَدٌ بِخَبَرِهِ
sentences.tr: wa-qāla la-qad zadtanī hamman ʿalā hammī wa-ghamman ʿalā ghammī fa-inna ibna ʿammika qalla ʿālimun wa-lā aʿlamu mā jarā ʿalayhi mundhu ayyāmin wa-lam yukhbirnī aḥadun bi-khabarihi
sentences.l: And he said: Indeed you have added to me a care upon my care, and a grief upon my grief; for indeed your cousin — rare is one who knows of him, and I do not know what has happened to him these days, and no one has told me news of him.
sentences.i: And he said: You have added a care to my care, and a grief to my grief — for as to your cousin, hardly anyone knows anything of him; even I do not know what has become of him these many days, nor has any man brought me word of him.
sentences.n: قَلَّ عَالِمٌ uses the classical idiom qalla + an indefinite subject, 'rare/few is [one who ...]', i.e. 'hardly anyone knows'.

sentences.t: وَبَكَي حَتَّى أُغْمِيَ عَلَيْهِ فَحَزِنْتُ عَلَيْهِ حُزْنًا شَدِيدًا
sentences.tr: wa-bakā ḥattā ughmiya ʿalayhi fa-ḥazintu ʿalayhi ḥuznan shadīdan
sentences.l: And he wept until he fainted, and I grieved for him a violent grief.
sentences.i: And he wept until he fell into a swoon, and I grieved bitterly for him.
sentences.n: The edition spells this verb وبكي with dotted yāʾ where the standard classical spelling of this final-weak verb (bakā, 'he wept') uses alif maqṣūra (بكى); vocalised here as the letters actually printed allow, with the intended reading bakā.

sentences.t: فَأَرَادَ أَنْ يَحُطَّ عَلَى عَيْنِي دَوَاءً فَرَآهَا صَارَتْ جَوْزَةً فَارِغَةً فَقَالَ يَا وَلَدِي بِعَيْنِكَ وَلَا بِرُوحِكَ
sentences.tr: fa-arāda an yaḥuṭṭa ʿalā ʿaynī dawāʾan fa-raʾāhā ṣārat jawzatan fārighatan fa-qāla yā waladī bi-ʿaynika wa-lā bi-rūḥika
sentences.l: So he wanted to put upon my eye a medicine; then he saw it — it had become an empty walnut; and he said: O my son, by your eye, and not by your soul.
sentences.i: So he meant to apply a remedy to my eye, but when he looked he found it had become like an empty walnut-shell; and he said, 'My son — better your eye than your life!'
sentences.n: بِعَيْنِكَ وَلَا بِرُوحِكَ, 'by your eye and not your soul', is a set consolation formula: count yourself lucky it cost only an eye, not a life.

sentences.t: قَالَ وَلَمْ يُمْكِنِي السُّكُوتُ عَلَى اِبْنِ عَمِّي الَّذِي هُوَ وَلَدُهُ فَأَعْلَمْتُهُ بِالَّذِي جَرَى كُلَّهُ
sentences.tr: qāla wa-lam yumkinī al-sukūtu ʿalā ibni ʿammī alladhī huwa waladuhu fa-aʿlamtuhu bi-alladhī jarā kullahu
sentences.l: He said: and silence was not possible for me concerning the son of my uncle, who is his own son; so I informed him of what had happened, all of it.
sentences.i: He continued: I could not keep silent about my cousin, who was his own son, and so I told him everything that had happened.
sentences.n: يُمْكِنِي is printed with a single نʹ where Classical grammar would double it before the 1cs suffix (يُمْكِنِّي); vocalised as the single letter printed allows, a Middle Arabic simplification.

sentences.t: فَفَرِحَ عَمِّي بِالَّذِي قُلْتُهُ لَهُ فَرَحًا شَدِيدًا عَنْ كُلِّ سَمَاعِ خَبَرِ اِبْنِهِ وَقَالَ قُمْ أِرِنِي التُّرْبَةَ
sentences.tr: fa-fariḥa ʿammī bi-alladhī qultuhu lahu faraḥan shadīdan ʿan kulli samāʿi khabari ibnihi wa-qāla qum arinī al-turbata
sentences.l: So my uncle rejoiced at what I had told him, a violent joy, above every hearing of news of his son; and he said: Rise, show me the tomb-enclosure.
sentences.i: My uncle rejoiced greatly at what I told him — more than at any other tidings of his son — and he said, 'Get up and show me the tomb-enclosure.'

sentences.t: فَقُلْتُ وَاللَّهِ يَا عَمِّي لَمْ أَعْرِفْ مَكَانَهَا لِأَنِّي رُحْتُ بَعْدَ ذَلِكَ مِرَارًا وَفَتَّشْتُ عَلَيْهَا فَلَمْ أَعْرِفْ مَكَانَهَا
sentences.tr: fa-qultu wa-Allāhi yā ʿammī lam aʿrif makānahā li-annī ruḥtu baʿda dhālika mirāran wa-fattashtu ʿalayhā fa-lam aʿrif makānahā
sentences.l: So I said: By God, O my uncle, I do not know its place, because I went, after that, many times, and I searched for it, so I did not know its place.
sentences.i: I said: By God, my uncle, I do not know where it is — for I went back many times after that and searched for it, but I could never find the place.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ أَتَيْتُ أَنَا وَعَمِّي إِلَى الْجَبَّانَةِ وَنَظَرْتُ يَمِينًا وَشِمَالًا فَعَرَفْتُهَا فَرِحْنَا أَنَا وَعَمِّي فَرَحًا شَدِيدًا
sentences.tr: thumma ataytu anā wa-ʿammī ilā al-jabbānati wa-naẓartu yamīnan wa-shimālan fa-ʿaraftuhā fariḥnā anā wa-ʿammī faraḥan shadīdan
sentences.l: Then I came, I and my uncle, to the burial-ground, and I looked right and left, so I recognized it; we rejoiced, I and my uncle, a violent joy.
sentences.i: Then my uncle and I went together to the burial-ground, and I looked right and left until I recognized it. We rejoiced, my uncle and I, exceedingly.

sentences.t: وَدَخَلْتُ أَنَا وَإِيَّاهُ التُّرْبَةَ وَشَلْنَا التُّرَابَ وَ رَفَعْنَا الطَّابِقَ وَنَزَلْتُ أَنَا وَعَمِّي قَدْرَ خَمْسِينَ دَرَجَةً
sentences.tr: wa-dakhaltu anā wa-iyyāhu al-turbata wa-shalnā al-turāba wa-rafaʿnā al-ṭābiqa wa-nazaltu anā wa-ʿammī qadra khamsīna darajatan
sentences.l: And I entered, I and he, the tomb-enclosure, and we cleared away the earth, and we lifted the slab, and I descended, I and my uncle, about fifty steps.
sentences.i: So he and I went down into the tomb-enclosure together; we cleared away the earth and lifted the flagstone, and my uncle and I went down some fifty steps.
sentences.n: شَلْنَا 'we removed/lifted' and الطَّابِقَ 'the slab' are colloquial usages (from shāla, 'to lift, carry off', and ṭābiq in the sense of a flagstone or trapdoor rather than a building storey).

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا وَصَلْنَا إِلَى آخِرِ سُلَّمٍ وَإِذَا بِدُخَانٍ طَلَعَ عَلَيْنَا حَتَّى غَشَى أَبْصَارَنَا فَقَالَ عَمِّي كَلِمَةً لَا يَخْجَلُ قَائِلُهَا لَا حَوْلَ وَلَا قُوَّةَ إِلَّا بِاللَّهِ الْعَلِيِّ الْعَظِيمِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā waṣalnā ilā ākhiri sullamin wa-idhā bi-dukhānin ṭalaʿa ʿalaynā ḥattā ghashā abṣāranā fa-qāla ʿammī kalimatan lā yakhjalu qāʾiluhā lā ḥawla wa-lā quwwata illā bi-Allāhi al-ʿaliyyi al-ʿaẓīmi
sentences.l: And when we reached the end of a ladder, and behold, with smoke that rose upon us until it covered our sights; and my uncle said a phrase its speaker is not ashamed of: There is no power and no strength except in God, the Most High, the Great.
sentences.i: When we reached the foot of the stair, all at once a smoke rose up and blinded our sight, and my uncle spoke a phrase no one need be ashamed to say: 'There is no power and no strength save in God, the Most High, the Almighty.'
sentences.n: وَإِذَا بِدُخَانٍ, 'and behold, with smoke': after wa-idhā of surprise, the bi- marks only what suddenly appears, not an instrument.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ مَشَيْنَا وَ إِذَا نَحْنُ بِقَاعَةٍ مَلَانَةٍ دَقِيقًا وَمِنَ الْحُبُوبِ وَالْمَأْكُولِ وَغَيْرِ ذَلِكَ وَ رَأَيْنَا فِي وَسَطِ الْقَاعَةِ بِشَخَّانَةٍ مُرْخَاةٍ عَلَى سَرِيرٍ
sentences.tr: thumma mashaynā wa-idhā naḥnu bi-qāʿatin malānatin daqīqan wa-min al-ḥubūbi wa-al-maʾkūli wa-ghayri dhālika wa-raʾaynā fī wasaṭi al-qāʿati bi-shakhkhānatin murkhātin ʿalā sarīrin
sentences.l: Then we walked, and behold, we were in a hall full of flour, and of grains, and food, and other than that; and we saw in the middle of the hall a [shakhkhāna] let down over a couch.
sentences.i: Then we walked on, and there we found ourselves in a chamber heaped with flour and grain and food and the like; and in the middle of the chamber we saw a canopy let down over a couch.
sentences.n: بِشَخَّانَةٍ is obscure; the word is not attested in the standard lexicons. It may denote some kind of canopy or curtained hood over the couch (perhaps related to a heating-vessel, shakhkhāna, 'a brazier', given the root sh-kh-n, 'to warm'), but the sense stays a guess. مَلَانَةٍ, 'full', is the colloquial form of the adjective, without the root hamza of Classical malʾā/mumtaliʾa.

sentences.t: فَنَظَرَ عَمِّي إِلَى السَّرِيرِ فَوَجِلَ اِبْنُهُ وَالْمَرْأَةُ الَّتِي قَدْ نَزَلَتْ مَعَهُ صَارَا فَحْمًا أَسْوَدَ وَهُمَا مُتَعَانِقَيْنِ كَأَنَّهُمَا أُلْقِيَا فِي جُبٍّ مِنْ نَارٍ
sentences.tr: fa-naẓara ʿammī ilā al-sarīri fa-wajila ibnuhu wa-al-marʾatu allatī qad nazalat maʿahu ṣārā faḥman aswada wa-humā mutaʿāniqayni ka-annahumā ulqiyā fī jubbin min nārin
sentences.l: So my uncle looked at the couch, and he was seized with terror: his son and the woman who had gone down with him — the two of them had become black coal, the two of them embracing, as though they had been cast into a pit of fire.
sentences.i: My uncle looked at the couch, and was struck with dread: his son and the woman who had gone down with him had both turned to black charcoal, locked in an embrace, as though the two of them had been cast into a pit of fire.
sentences.n: فَوَجِلَ, 'and he was terrified', is intransitive: what follows (اِبْنُهُ وَالْمَرْأَةُ ... صَارَا) is the sight that caused his terror, not its grammatical object.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا نَظَرَ عَمِّي ذَلِكَ بَزَقَ فِي وَجْهِهِ وَقَالَ تَسْتَاهِلُ يَا خِنْزِيرُ هٰذَا عَذَابُ الدُّنْيَا وَبَقِيَ عَذَابُ الْآخِرَةِ أَشَدُّ وَأَقْوَى
sentences.tr: fa-lammā naẓara ʿammī dhālika bazaqa fī wajhihi wa-qāla tastāhilu yā khinzīru hādhā ʿadhābu al-dunyā wa-baqiya ʿadhābu al-ākhirati ashaddu wa-aqwā
sentences.l: And when my uncle saw that, he spat in its face and said: You deserve it, O swine — this is the punishment of this world, and there remains the punishment of the hereafter, more severe and stronger.
sentences.i: When my uncle saw this, he spat in the corpse's face and said, 'This serves you right, you swine — this is the punishment of this world; there remains still the punishment of the world to come, more severe and more terrible.'
sentences.n: تَسْتَاهِلُ, 'you deserve [it]', is the colloquial form of the Classical تَسْتَأْهِلُ.

sentences.t: وَأَدْرَكَ شَهْرَزَادَ الصَّبَاحُ فَسَكَتَتْ عَنِ الْكَلَامِ الْمُبَاحِ
sentences.tr: wa-adraka Shahrazāda al-ṣabāḥu fa-sakatat ʿani al-kalāmi al-mubāḥi
sentences.l: And dawn overtook Shahrazad, and she fell silent from the permitted speech.
sentences.i: And dawn overtook Shahrazad, so she fell silent, leaving unsaid what she still had leave to tell.
